fixes.explanation: No warning is mentioned in the text, baker. What it does say is that seeing it pleased the Jews, Herod "…proceeded to seize Peter…" (Acts 12:3). Peter is one of Jesus' twelve apostles (Matthew 10:2). The arrest is what comes next.

The Sabbath isn't named in the verse, friend. Acts 12:4 says Herod "…intended to bring him out to the people after the Passover." The arrest happened during the Feast of Unleavened Bread (Acts 12:3), so the Passover is the one on the calendar here.

It's a natural guess, baker, since Acts 12:5 says the church was fervently praying to God for him. But about Peter that night, the text says he was "…sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains…" (Acts 12:6). Peter is the one who's asleep.
True, baker. The angel tells him, "Get up quickly." Then "…the chains fell off his wrists." (Acts 12:7). Two chains were holding him (Acts 12:6), and they came off.

You got it, baker. Acts 12:9 says Peter followed the angel out, "…but he was unaware that what the angel was doing was real. He thought he was only seeing a vision." So he's walking out of prison and thinks it's only a vision. I'd be pinching myself the whole way.
Fair guess, friend, but a trap isn't mentioned in the text. Acts 12:9 says Peter "…thought he was only seeing a vision." The verse also says he "…was unaware that what the angel was doing was real."
Yes, baker! Acts 12:10 says they passed the first and second guards and came to the iron gate leading to the city, which "…opened for them by itself." Then they went outside. That's some gate.
That's a fun picture, friend, but the text doesn't say it. Acts 12:10 says the iron gate "…opened for them by itself." The verse says nothing about a lock being broken.

A guard unlocking it isn't in the text, baker. Acts 12:10 says they passed the first and second guards, and then the iron gate "…opened for them by itself." The verse gives the gate itself as the one doing the opening.

No, baker. Peter's own words in Acts 12:11 are, "Now I know for sure that the Lord has sent His angel and rescued me…" Peter credits the Lord, not the guards. And the soldiers are in "…no small commotion…" about what became of him (Acts 12:18).
That isn't what Peter says, friend. He says the Lord "…rescued me from Herod’s grasp…" (Acts 12:11). Later Herod searched for him unsuccessfully (Acts 12:19). Peter names the Lord as his rescuer.

That would be the sensible move, friend, but it's not what happens. Rhoda was so overjoyed that she "…forgot to open the gate, but ran inside…" (Acts 12:14). Then she announces that Peter is standing at the gate. Meanwhile Peter kept on knocking (Acts 12:16).

Astounded, baker! Acts 12:16 says Peter kept on knocking, and when they opened the door and saw him, "…they were astounded." Earlier they had told Rhoda, "You are out of your mind," (Acts 12:15). He was standing right there at the door, just like Rhoda said.
Furious isn't the word the text uses, friend. Acts 12:16 says that when they opened the door and saw Peter, "…they were astounded." They'd been praying (Acts 12:12), and now he's in front of them.

Disappointed isn't the word the text uses, baker. Acts 12:16 says that when they finally opened the door and saw Peter, "…they were astounded." Peter had kept on knocking, and now he's standing in front of them.
No, friend. Acts 12:17 says Peter "…left for another place." Later Herod searched for him unsuccessfully (Acts 12:19). The text never has Peter going back to Herod.

No, baker. Acts 12:19 says that after searching for Peter unsuccessfully, Herod "…examined the guards and ordered that they be executed." Being sent home isn't what the verse says. It's a heavy verse, and I think it's one to read slowly.

Food, baker. Acts 12:20 says Herod was in a "…furious dispute with the people of Tyre and Sidon…" and they asked for peace "…because their region depended on the king’s country for food." Tyre and Sidon needed what Herod's country supplied, so they weren't about to stay in a fight.
A prophet speaks for God, friend (2 Peter 1:21), and that's not what they shout. Acts 12:22 says, "This is the voice of a god, not a man!" They called Herod's voice a god's voice.

Herod already is a king, so this would have been a smaller compliment, baker. The text calls him King Herod right from the start (Acts 12:1). The crowd shouts something bigger: "This is the voice of a god, not a man!" (Acts 12:22).
Jerusalem, baker. Acts 12:25 says Barnabas and Saul "…had fulfilled their mission to Jerusalem…" and then returned. They brought John, also called Mark, back with them.

Damascus sounds official, friend, but I can't find it anywhere in this passage. Acts 12:25 says Barnabas and Saul "…had fulfilled their mission to Jerusalem…" before they returned. Jerusalem is the stop on their map.

Tarsus would be a trip, baker, but the verse names a different place. Acts 12:25 says Barnabas and Saul "…had fulfilled their mission to Jerusalem…" Then they returned, bringing John, also called Mark.
